title: Mission: check your own accounts
drDigitalIntro:
A fake site can copy a real one perfectly — the logo, the layout, the wording, all of it. The one thing it cannot copy is the address in the bar at the top.
• You will read this page's real address out of that bar and type it back, because that is the habit that catches nearly every phishing attempt.
• Then you will do the two things that actually protect an account: two-factor authentication on the important one, and no reused passwords.
• Reused passwords are the single biggest risk most people carry. One leak somewhere becomes a break-in everywhere.
• None of this is checked by the page except the first step. It is checked by you not being burgled.

playgroundTask.goal: You checked the address bar and hardened a real account

steps.say: Read the address bar and type the address this page is really at.
steps.detail: The part before the first slash. A convincing fake will have a convincing page and an address that is slightly wrong — an extra word, a different ending, a zero for an o.

steps.say: Turn on two-factor authentication for your most important account.
steps.detail: Email first, because everything else resets through it. Two-factor means a stolen password on its own is not enough to get in.

steps.say: Change any password you use in more than one place.
steps.detail: Start with the ones attached to money or email. Three unrelated words with a number is easier to remember and harder to break than Passw0rd!

steps.say: Find the last suspicious message you received and check the sender's real address.
steps.detail: The display name is decoration and anyone can set it. The address behind it is the fact. They almost never match on a scam.

drDigitalSuccess: You read a real address bar and did the two things that actually protect an account. Most people never do either.
drDigitalHint: For the first step, ignore everything on the page and read the strip at the very top of the browser window.
